reader.title: Lynchings of religious reformers in central Arkansas (1880)
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: Two Little Rock dispatches describe murders attributed to followers of a religious reformation in central Arkansas in 1880 as followed by 'a series of lynchings' of the men implicated (A2, A3, A5).

The dispatches say the men implicated in the murders were lynched, 'summarily dealt with' after the killings 'aroused the neighborhood' (A2, A3), which implies illegal killings in retaliation for alleged crimes; but they name no victims, perpetrators, number, date or place, and are a retrospective aside in reports about Matlock (A2, A5).

Two separate Little Rock specials, the New York/Chicago version (A2, A5) and the St. Louis Republican version (A3), both state that the murders were followed by lynchings, though both are brief retrospective mentions without local detail.

summary.text: The lynchings of religious reformers in central Arkansas were a series of killings in 1880 of men implicated in murders attributed to a religious reformation that had begun there that summer.
They are known only from brief retrospective passages in April 1881 wire reports about Rev. Robert Matlock, one of the movement's leaders, which named none of the men lynched.
The dispatches credited the lynchings with having ended the movement.

According to a Little Rock special printed in the Chicago Tribune, Matlock and several others began in the summer of 1880 a religious reformation in a number of counties in central Arkansas that created intense excitement and drove many people insane.
One of its doctrines, the dispatches said, was that the shedding of human blood was necessary to appease an offended God.

The Chicago text said this doctrine bore fruit in the murder of three or four innocent persons by some of the reformers or their followers, whose heads were severed and set on poles in the woods; the St. Louis Republican's special said only that it was alleged that several murders resulted.
The killings aroused the neighborhood where they occurred and led to a series of lynchings in which all the male persons implicated were summarily dealt with.
Matlock, whose guilt was not clearly established, escaped.
The reports give no names, number, date, place or method for the lynchings.
No report of arrests, an inquest or a trial for the lynchings appears in the coverage.
According to the St. Louis Republican's special, the lynchings effectually checked the further progress of the religious frenzy.

Matlock himself was charged with stabbing a planter, Thomas Miller, at a barbecue in Independence County in August 1880 and was acquitted in Lawrence County; in April 1881 a body supposed to be his was reported found hanging from a tree in Izard county.
In October 1881 papers reported that he had not been lynched and had been seen near Corsicana, Texas.
The lynchings reached print only as background to the Matlock story, which ran in two versions of a Little Rock special.
The longer version appeared in the Chicago Tribune under 'A Notorious Clergyman Lynched' and in the Wheeling Intelligencer and Omaha Bee on April 22, the Bee headlining it 'A Lynched Lunatic'.

The St. Louis Republican's version ran in the Memphis Appeal and Wheeling Register on April 21, the Gold Hill Daily News on April 22 as 'Religion and Retribution', and the Belmont Chronicle and New Hampshire Patriot on April 28.
Neither version gave the lynchings more than a sentence or two, and both presented them as a remedy for the 'religious frenzy' rather than as crimes; no racial terms appear in either.

The Wheeling Intelligencer alone placed the murders 'in Burke county', at the point where the Chicago Tribune's printing of the same New York text reads 'the brutal murder', and the Intelligencer also turned Lawrence county into 'Luzerne county'.
The count of the murdered differed between 'three or four' and 'several', and no version described them as children.

accounts.label: Little Rock special (New York/Chicago version)
accounts.gist: The reformers' blood doctrine 'bore fruit' in the murder of three or four persons whose heads were put on poles; the neighborhood responded with a series of lynchings of all male persons implicated, and Matlock escaped.

accounts.label: Little Rock special to the St. Louis Republican
accounts.gist: It was 'alleged' that several murders resulted from the reformers' teachings, and these were 'supplemented by a series of lynchings' that checked the religious movement.

framing.detail: The lynchings are an aside credited with having 'effectually checked' the 'religious frenzy'; headlines concern Matlock ('A Notorious Clergyman Lynched', 'A Lynched Lunatic', 'Religion and Retribution').
The two Little Rock specials ran across the country from Chicago and Memphis to Wheeling, Omaha, Nevada, Ohio and New Hampshire between April 21 and 28, 1881.

conflicts.note: None of the texts says the murdered persons were children.

versions.value: 'a number of counties in Central Arkansas', no county named

conflicts.note: 'Burke county' appears only in the Wheeling Intelligencer, at the point where the parallel New York text in the Chicago Tribune reads 'bore fruit in the brutal murder' (the Omaha Bee copy also has 'brutal murder'); the same text renders Lawrence county as 'Luzerne county'. It is most likely a garble, not a place.

record_check.dossier: Men implicated in murders attributed to an 1880 religious reformation in central Arkansas were lynched; 'Burke county' is a garble of 'brutal murder' and no children are mentioned.
1880 (after the reformation began in summer 1880), reported in retrospect April 1881; the record's April 1881 placement reflects the report date.
Not stated in any text; nothing indicates the lynched men were Black.

info: Not given; the reformation began in the summer of 1880 ('a year ago' as of April 1881), and the murders and lynchings followed; reported in retrospect April 20-22, 1881.
'a number of counties in Central Arkansas'; 'the neighborhood in which they occurred'; no county named except a garbled 'Burke county' in one text.
Unnamed: 'all the male persons implicated' in the murders, i.e. 'some of the reformers or their deluded followers'; race not stated.

Murder of 'three or four innocent persons' (A2) or 'several' (A3, A5), said to follow a doctrine that shedding human blood was needed to appease God; heads of the dead were severed and set on poles in the woods.
Not identified; the murders 'aroused the neighborhood' and led to the lynchings.
The lynchings 'effectually checked the further progress of the religious frenzy'; Rev. Robert Matlock, whose guilt was 'not being clearly established', escaped.
